extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and students seeking an encyclopedic overview of the DHS Disinformation Governance Board
extracted.subtask_short: encyclopedic entry on DHS disinformation board
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedia article summarizing the Disinformation Governance Board: its formation, stated function, scope, leadership, reactions, and dissolution. Useful for readers seeking a neutral overview of the board and controversies surrounding it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stated purpose: protect national security by combating misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The board's stated function was to protect national security by disseminating guidance to DHS agencies on combating misinformation, malinformation, and disinformation that threatens the security of the homeland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites DHS wording and examples of problem areas (e.g., false information from human smugglers encouraging migrants to surge to the Mexico–United States border; Russian-state disinformation on election interference and the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory role and coordination (no operational authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The board would serve as an advisory body and help coordinate anti-disinformation efforts throughout the department; it would have no operational authority or capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS officials emphasized the board would collect best practices for dissemination to DHS organizations already tasked with defending against disinformation threats; John Cohen described the board as studying policy questions, best practices, and academic research, then submitting guidance to the DHS secretary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit limitation: will not monitor American citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS asserted the board would not monitor American citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation is repeatedly noted in statements defending the board, and was highlighted by Secretary Mayorkas ("The Department is deeply committed to doing all of its work in a way that protects Americans' freedom of speech, civil rights, civil liberties, and privacy").

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of disinformation threats to be addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: The board would monitor disinformation spread by foreign states (such as Russia, China, and Iran), transnational criminal organizations and human smuggling organizations, and disinformation spread during natural disasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS gave concrete examples (e.g., misinformation about drinking water safety during Hurricane Sandy) and named target threat actors (foreign states, transnational criminal organizations, human smugglers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of civil liberties, privacy, and freedom of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department stated a commitment that the board's work would protect Americans' freedom of speech, civil rights, civil liberties, and privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as an explicit constraint on board activities and was used as part of public defense against criticism about potential censorship or overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and oversight: quarterly reports to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The DGB announced that it would provide quarterly reports to the United States Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic reporting to Congress is presented as a transparency and accountability mechanism for the board's advisory activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and clear public communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The board needed clear communication of its mission and purpose; failures by DHS to communicate contributed to criticism and a "bungled rollout."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques cited DHS's failure to communicate with relevant congressional entities and to clearly explain the board's name and mission; page highlights statements that DHS could have done a better job communicating the purpose of the board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and public perception considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The board's name and how it is presented to the public affect public trust; a poorly chosen name can inspire suspicion or conspiracy narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media commentary stated the board's name did not inspire confidence and contributed to misrepresentation and backlash (e.g., comparisons to Orwell's "Ministry of Truth").

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership qualifications and perceived partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership appointments should be qualified and perceived as nonpartisan; past public statements by leaders were treated as grounds for criticism of suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nina Jankowicz's prior affiliations and social media comments were central to critiques; commentators and lawmakers questioned whether her background and statements made her an appropriate, impartial leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to avoid government policing of speech given DHS enforcement powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because DHS has enforcement powers, involvement in decisions surrounding speech raises First Amendment and civil-liberties concerns; the board must avoid becoming a 'truth police' or exercising enforcement over speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts and commentators warned it would be 'wrong and concerning' for an agency with enforcement powers to be involved in speech decisions; legal and constitutional implications were central to public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to build public trust and defend against disinformation about the board itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The board needed to actively build public trust and defend its own mission from disinformation and misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators described the board as a 'victim of disinformation' and emphasized that inadequate communication and transparency allowed conspiracy theories and false claims (e.g., about editing private Twitter posts) to spread.
